16791178_a7f71829.text: The orexins, named for the Greek word for appetite (Sakurai et al., 1998), stimulate appetite (Sakurai et al., 1998) and are the common name given to the neuropeptide and the neurotransmitter (Lecea et al., 1998) called orexin-A and orexin-B (also known as hypocretin-1 [HCRT-[1] and hypocretin-2 [HCRT-[2]) (Sakurai et al., 1998)(Sakurai, 2007)

16791178_c011c4bd.text: . Orexins are produced by neurons mainly located in the lateral hypothalamic area (Sakurai et al., 1998)(Gotter et al., 2012). These neurons send widespread projections into the prefrontal cortex, hippocampus, thalamus, and hypothalamus (Peyron et al., 1998). Orexin neurons also play crucial roles in the regulation of sleep and wakefulness (Sakurai et al., 1998)(Armitage, 2007)(Steiger et al., 2010), appetite (Luppino et al., 2010)(Stunkard et al., 2003)(Dube et al., 1999), and energy homeostasis (Sakurai et al., 2011). Orexin neurons detect nutritional status by reacting to peripheral metabolic signals such as glucose and appetite-related hormones (leptin and ghrelin) [76][77][78] and controlling the production glucose [79][80][81] and vital gases [82], and also receive the various neural signal inputs [83].
